issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, 'Babies' as a salient auditory trigger is hard to connect clinically unless the accident specifically involved infants/crying, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger items (intrusive thoughts, nightmare residue) are generic trauma reactivation cues, making this item stand out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Make sure never to be alone with another person' suggests avoidance linked to fear of being accused of harming someone or of interpersonal/sexual threat, which is not coherently supported by the accident trauma type, threat items, or appraisals. The rest of the profile is organized around generalized danger/vulnerability, not being alone with another person specifically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after an accident, but here it lacks support from the other selected items. The threat and strategy items focus on physical danger and hypervigilance, while no memory or trigger content suggests shame-based social exposure. In this profile, humiliation is the least coherent appraisal and appears disconnected from the accident-focused formulation.

vignette: Thanh, a 33-year-old South Eastern Asian male and married physical therapist, experienced a life-threatening accident that has profoundly impacted his daily life. The accident occurred while he was driving home from work late one evening. A sudden loud noise, like an explosion in the distance, made him swerve and lose control of the car, sending it off the road and into a ditch. Miraculously, Thanh survived but sustained severe injuries that required extensive medical treatment. Since then, Thanh has been plagued by intrusive thoughts about the accident. These unwanted memories often surface during mundane activities at work or while he's with his family. For example, when he hears a loud noise, such as a car backfiring in his neighborhood, it immediately triggers vivid recollections of the explosion that led to the crash. He wakes up from nightmares frequently, feeling disoriented and distressed. Thanh's maladaptive strategies have become increasingly pronounced over time. He compulsively cleans or organizes things repeatedly, believing this gives him a sense of control in an otherwise unpredictable world. This behavior extends even into his professional life as a physical therapist; he meticulously arranges the therapy equipment each morning, ensuring nothing is out of place. Additionally, he mentally rehearses worst-case scenarios to feel prepared for any potential threats. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of danger, particularly noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects. His concentration has been significantly impaired by these heightened vigilance and threat-monitoring behaviors. At work, this manifests as difficulty focusing on patient care, leading to occasional mistakes in treatment plans. His startle response is also pronounced; even small movements can make him jump suddenly, which often causes discomfort among his patients and colleagues who notice his increased anxiety. Thanh's negative appraisals have further compounded his distress. He has come to believe that his body has been permanently damaged by the accident, making him feel vulnerable and weak. This fear of harm extends beyond physical threats; he is now convinced that anyone could pose a danger at any moment. As a result, he struggles to trust others, even those closest to him, including his spouse. The combination of these symptoms has led to significant changes in Thanh's life. His compulsive cleaning and constant vigilance have strained his relationships with colleagues and family members. His wife often expresses concern about his behavior but feels helpless when she sees how much it distresses him. Recently, the cumulative impact of his symptoms became too overwhelming for Thanh to ignore. He found himself unable to perform basic tasks at work without being distracted by intrusive thoughts or feeling jumpy. The realization that he needed help to regain control over his life and improve his relationships finally brought him to seek psychological treatment. Thanh is most afraid of never regaining a sense of normalcy and security in his life. He hopes that through therapy, he can learn strategies to manage his symptoms more effectively and regain trust not only in himself but also in the world around him.
